analysis.one_liner: Makes the 2001 and 2003 tax cuts permanent and permanently repeals the estate tax.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on November 17, 2010 and never received a hearing, a vote, or floor action before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2001 and 2003 tax laws cut income tax rates, the marriage penalty, the child credit, and taxes on dividends and capital gains, but were written to expire at the end of 2010. This bill would strike those expiration dates, making every provision permanent. It would also repeal the estate tax outright, permanently raise the exemption amounts for the alternative minimum tax (a parallel tax that hits middle- and upper-middle-income families who claim many deductions), and let more tax credits count against the AMT. It would also end, after 2011, the Affordable Care Act's expanded adoption tax benefits.
analysis.who_benefits: High-income households gain the most in dollars: the bill makes permanent the cuts to the top income tax rates and to the tax rates on dividends and capital gains, and it repeals the estate tax entirely, a benefit only available to the largest estates. Middle-income families gain too, from permanently extended rate cuts, child credits, and marriage-penalty relief, and from permanent AMT relief.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners and heirs of large estates

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the expiration date of the 2001 tax law (EGTRRA), making its income tax rate cuts, child tax credit, and marriage penalty relief permanent [S2][S3].
Repeals the expiration date of the 2003 tax law (JGTRRA), keeping the reduced tax rates on dividends and capital gains in place permanently [S2][S3].
Permanently repeals the estate tax, so no estate would owe federal estate tax regardless of size [S3].

Permanently raises the alternative minimum tax exemption amounts, phasing in through 2020 to $109,950 for joint filers and $66,200 for single filers, and lets nonrefundable credits such as the child tax credit offset the AMT [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal treasury bears the cost, meaning future taxpayers through larger deficits, because the provisions were originally written with expiration dates to limit their cost under budget rules. Middle- and upper-middle-income families gain AMT relief and extended rates, but the largest dollar benefits go to the highest earners and the largest estates. Adoptive families lose the Affordable Care Act's expanded adoption tax benefits after 2011.

drawbacks.text: The bill permanently repeals the estate tax, which applied only to the largest estates; under the law in effect for 2009, estates above a $3.5 million exemption owed tax [S3].
It terminates the Affordable Care Act's increased tax benefits for adoption after December 31, 2011, taking away a benefit the ACA had provided to adoptive families [S2][S3].

The 2001 and 2003 tax cuts were written with expiration dates (sunsets); eliminating them means the revenue those dates were designed to return never comes back, adding to deficits indefinitely [S2][S3].

The permanent extensions include the reduced top income tax rates and the 15% rate on dividends and capital gains, the provisions whose dollar benefits are concentrated among the highest-income households [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The middle-class pieces — extended rates, child credits, and the permanent AMT fix — are real and widely felt; the AMT in particular threatened millions of families who never considered themselves wealthy. But the bill bundles those with its costliest provisions: permanent repeal of the estate tax and permanent lock-in of the top-rate and investment-income cuts, which flow overwhelmingly to the wealthiest households. It also takes away the ACA's expanded adoption benefits after 2011. The whole package, made permanent rather than extended temporarily, would have added substantially to federal deficits. A narrower bill limited to the middle-class and AMT provisions would have been far cheaper and less skewed.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the final weeks of the 111th Congress and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2011 with no vote at any stage.

narrative.text: Representative Mike Pence (R-IN) introduced the bill on November 17, 2010, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day [S1][S5].
Twenty-six House Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrats did [S4].
No further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — appears in the bill's action history, and the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S5].

Three weeks after introduction, in December 2010, President Obama and congressional Republican leaders negotiated a separate law that extended the 2001 and 2003 tax cuts for two years and set the estate tax at a 35% rate with a $5 million exemption, rather than making them permanent.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners and large estates came out ahead of the bill's death only in a limited sense: they kept their tax cuts for two more years through the December 2010 compromise anyway, while the bill's permanent estate tax repeal — the provision that would have gone furthest for the wealthiest households — never took effect. Middle-income families got their extensions and, unlike under the bill, retained the ACA's expanded adoption benefits.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners, via the two-year extension compromise

for.name: Mike Pence
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on November 17, 2010 to permanently extend the 2001 and 2003 tax cuts and repeal the estate tax.

against.name: Sander Levin
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup or vote; the record shows no committee action after the referral.

against.name: Barack Obama
against.what_they_did: Negotiated a December 2010 compromise with congressional Republican leaders extending the 2001 and 2003 tax cuts for two years rather than permanently, making the bill moot.

sides.party_line_note: All 26 cosponsors were Republicans, and the bill died without action in a committee chaired by a Democrat; the substance was later handled through a December 2010 compromise between a Democratic president and Republican congressional leaders.

industries.note: The bill repeals the estate tax entirely, wiping out a tax that fell only on estates above the exemption threshold — under 2009 law, above $3.5 million. The benefit is unavailable to estates below that size, so it is concentrated among the wealthiest families.

Making the 2001 and 2003 cuts permanent locks in the reduced top income tax rates and the 15% rates on dividends and capital gains, provisions whose dollar savings are largest for households with high salaries and large investment income. Middle-income families also benefit from the rate extensions, but far less in dollars.

industries.industry: Estate planning and wealth advisory firms
industries.note: Permanent certainty on low rates and AMT exemption amounts reduces the year-to-year planning churn caused by temporary tax provisions, making long-term planning for wealthy clients simpler and more predictable.
